dialogue.speaker: Greta Morrow
dialogue.content: I'm Greta — your mother, though I shouldn't have to introduce myself in my own kitchen. Coffee's on. The good stuff, not that instant powder you brought back from Chicago that tastes like it was brewed through a newspaper.

dialogue.speaker: Casey Morrow
dialogue.content: I'm Casey. Your child. The one who used to drink that 'newspaper coffee' every morning and call it sophisticated. Remember?

dialogue.speaker: Greta Morrow
dialogue.content: I remember a lot of things. Like how you used to sit at this same table and tell me about all the places you'd go. You had a list. New York. San Francisco. London, once, after you saw that documentary about the BBC. Said you were going to work in radio, make people feel things with your voice.

dialogue.speaker: Casey Morrow
dialogue.content: I did work in radio. Public radio. I produced segments. Interviewed people. Made them feel heard.

dialogue.speaker: Greta Morrow
dialogue.content: I know. I listened to every single one. Stayed up late sometimes, streaming that Chicago station on my phone until the data ran out. Your father too, before he passed. He wouldn't admit it, but I'd catch him in the garage, listening to you interview some poet or politician or whoever, and he'd have that look on his face — like he was proud of something he didn't quite understand.

dialogue.speaker: Casey Morrow
dialogue.content: Mom —

dialogue.speaker: Greta Morrow
dialogue.content: I'm not saying anything. Just remembering. That's allowed, isn't it? Speaking of — I ran into Darlene Kowalski at church yesterday. You remember Darlene. Her daughter Melissa got on at that call center out by the highway. Good benefits. Steady hours. They're still hiring, if you can believe it. In this economy.

dialogue.speaker: Casey Morrow
dialogue.content: A call center. You want me to work at a call center. After everything I —

dialogue.speaker: Greta Morrow
dialogue.content: I don't want anything. I'm just passing along information. You can do whatever you want with it. You always have.

dialogue.speaker: Casey Morrow
dialogue.content: I'm waiting to hear back about something. A position. In Cincinnati. It's not — it's not the dream job, but it's connected. It's a thread.

dialogue.speaker: Greta Morrow
dialogue.content: Then you wait. That's all any of us can do. But honey — waiting isn't the same as standing still. Even if it feels like it sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: Casey Morrow
dialogue.content: Ask Greta for more details about the call center position. Maybe stability isn't surrender.

*Greta's hand moves to the necklace at her throat, the twin birthstones catching morning light. Her coffee cup pauses halfway to her lips.*

It's customer service. Insurance claims, mostly. Melissa says the training takes three weeks. After that, you're on the phones. Twelve dollars an hour to start, but there's a raise at six months if you keep your metrics up. They've got a dental plan that's better than mine, I'll tell you that much.

*She sets the cup down, studies the formica as if it holds something she's trying to read.*

Your father worked at that plant for thirty-one years. It wasn't glamorous. Wasn't even interesting, most days. But it paid for this house. Put food on the table. Sent you and Brenda to college, even if you both did different things with it.

*She finally meets Casey's eyes — and there's something raw underneath the practical recitation, something that looks almost like grief.*

I'm not saying take the job. I'm saying — I watch you sit in that room every morning, staring at that phone like it owes you an apology. And I remember being twenty-seven. I remember how long a year can feel when you're waiting for something that might not come.

*Her voice drops, almost to herself.*

I just want you to have options. That's all I've ever wanted.

The rehearsal dinner's at the VFW hall. Brenda wanted the country club, but Derek's family wasn't going to pay those prices, and honestly, the hall's got better parking anyway. Your sister's been over the seating chart three times. I told her to leave it alone or she'd drive herself crazy.

*She pulls a folded piece of paper from her back pocket — the reception itinerary, edges already soft from handling.*

You're at Table Seven. With the Piechowski cousins and that friend of Derek's from the plant. Robby. Ricky? Something with an R. He's single, in case Brenda hasn't mentioned it. Fourteen times.

*The joke lands soft, an offering. A truce.*

She's been asking if you need anything for the ceremony. Hair, makeup — there's a woman coming to the house Saturday morning, doing everyone's. Brenda paid for you already. She didn't want you to worry about it.

*Greta's thumb traces the itinerary's edge.*

She's trying, Casey. In her way.

*The floorboard by the pantry groans. Brenda's shoulders freeze mid-turn, the muffin suspended in her hand.*

*She doesn't look back right away. A beat passes — two — and then she sets the burnt one aside with deliberate care.*

You're up early.

*Her voice is lighter than the moment warrants, already reaching for normalcy like a lifeline. She wipes her palms on the stolen sweatshirt, turns. Her face carries that particular expression of someone who's been rehearsing what to say and just had the script yanked away.*

*The friendship bracelet on her wrist catches the light — faded navy and white threads, the same pattern as the one you threw in a dumpster behind your apartment building three years ago.*

Mom said you might be coming down. She didn't say when.

*She gestures at the muffins, the movement too quick, covering something.*

I made too many. Obviously. Derek's mom is bringing the floral arrangements by noon and I still need to confirm the DJ and I can't find the — anyway. Muffins.

*Her eyes flick to your face, then away. Searching for something. Not finding it, or finding too much.*

You want one? They're not all burnt.

Good choice. That batch didn't sink.

*She leans against the counter, arms crossing over her chest. The movement's casual, practiced. But her fingers drum against her elbow — a nervous tell you remember from high school debate team finals, from the time she crashed her dad's Honda and pretended everything was fine.*

*The kitchen clock ticks its four-minutes-ahead rhythm. Outside, a truck rumbles past on Main Street. Somewhere deeper in the house, floorboards creak — Greta, probably, giving you space or finding reasons not to intrude.*

*The silence stretches. Brenda's eyes drop to the muffin in your hand, then back up. Her jaw tightens, relaxes.*

So.

*The word lands like a starting gun.*

Mom said you're... you're thinking about Cincinnati. That there's a call center. Data entry, something like that.

*She picks at the friendship bracelet — a reflex, maybe unconscious.*

I didn't know you were considering coming back. You didn't — I mean, we haven't really talked about it. Any of it.

How long has that been on the table?

*And then the landline rings.*

*It's a jarring, shrill thing — the bird-trapped-in-walls sound your father described once. Brenda flinches. Her hand drops from the bracelet. Neither of you moves.*

*One ring. Two. Three.*

That call center —

*Brenda's eyes stay fixed on you.*

We used to talk about Chicago. You and me. That summer before everything — you were going to apply to Northwestern's journalism program. You had the brochure pinned to your ceiling.

Why didn't you ever call me back?
